title: The Gurus answer Farid
hook: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan added their own saloks among Farid's, answering him gently

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid's crows and his plea: spare the eyes, I still hope. Today, someone answers Farid, centuries after he spoke.

An old book, passed down in a family. In the margin, a grandfather once wrote: life is hard, I've wasted my years. Decades later, a grandchild wrote beside it: not wasted, it isn't too late. Two people, perhaps strangers, talking across the page. The Guru Granth Sahib has pages like that. Beside Farid's saloks sit a few short verses marked with the Gurus' names, and read together, they turn out to be replies.
screen: `AN OLD FAMILY BOOK.` → `NOTES IN THE MARGIN.` → `TWO PEOPLE, TALKING ACROSS TIME.`

segments.voice: Among Sheikh Farid's saloks, the Guru Granth Sahib sets a handful by the Gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan. Each is marked with its Mahala, so you always know who's speaking. Some pick up Farid's exact words and turn them, gently. Here are two, in paraphrase. Farid says: those who didn't love the Lord when their hair was black, hardly anyone manages it once the hair turns white. So love the Lord, and your color will be ever new. It sounds like a warning: you may already be too late. Guru Amar Das answers, starting with Farid's own name: Farid, black hair or white, the Lord is always there, if anyone remembers. And love like that isn't won by effort alone, however much we long; it comes as a gift, by grace. Not too late: the Lord is there at every age. Elsewhere Farid, in his longing, says: my body burns like an oven, my bones burn like firewood; if my feet grow tired, I'll walk on my head to meet my Beloved. Guru Nanak answers: don't heat your body like an oven, don't burn your bones. What have your head and feet done wrong? See your Beloved within. Listen to the tone. The Gurus don't mock Farid or correct him coldly. They honor his longing, then open a softer door. That's how the book is built: not one voice lecturing, but a conversation across centuries, held with respect.
screen: `MARKED BY MAHALA — WHO'S SPEAKING.` · `FARID: TOO LATE, HAIR TURNED WHITE.` · `AMAR DAS: NEVER TOO LATE — GRACE.` · `NANAK: SEE THE BELOVED WITHIN.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION ACROSS CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: Think of someone older than you, a parent, a grandparent, an old teacher, a neighbor, and something they often say that you see differently. Picture answering them the way the Gurus answered Farid: first honoring what's true in it, then offering your view softly, by name, with respect.
Mahala, the mark of which Guru speaks. Among Farid's saloks, Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan add gentle replies, honoring his longing and opening a softer door.
Your line: a conversation across centuries. Even a disagreement can begin with honor. That's day two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib, each salok is marked with its author, so readers of Farid's saloks can see where Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan reply, and Sikh commentaries read them as a dialogue.

what it means: in the Granth, the Gurus reply to Farid within his own saloks, with respect, turning his words toward grace.
what a scholar hears: among the saloks in Farid's section, some are by the Gurus (Mahala 1, 3 and 5), often echoing Farid's opening words; a dialogic structure within the compiled text.

The outline names Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan; the script adds Guru Nanak because the best-known reply (the oven salok, 'see your Beloved within') is usually marked Mahala 1. Confirm the attributions and Angs (Farid 13 / M3 on Ang 1378; Farid 119 / M1 on Ang 1384).
